### Problem: Transpose matrix {#sec-mat-p2-transpose}

::: {.p-statement}
Given an $m \times n$ matrix, return its transpose: an $n \times m$ matrix whose row $j$ is the original column $j$, i.e. $\text{out}[j][i] = \text{in}[i][j]$.

$1 \le m, n \le 1000$ and $1 \le m \cdot n \le 10^5$; cells are integers. `[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]` transposes to `[[1,4],[2,5],[3,6]]`. `[[1,2],[3,4]]` transposes to `[[1,3],[2,4]]`.

Source: [LC 867 · Transpose Matrix](https://leetcode.com/problems/transpose-matrix/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The transpose mirrors the grid across its main diagonal: the value at row $i$, column $j$ moves to row $j$, column $i$ (@sec-mat-a3). The input may be rectangular, so the output has a different shape ($n$ rows of length $m$) and must be a new grid — the in-place swap works only for squares.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Nested build.** Allocate an $n \times m$ grid and write `T[j][i] = a[i][j]` for every input cell — the definition turned into code.
2. **Column zip.** Let Python gather each output row straight from an input column: `zip(*a)` hands over the $j$-th element of every row together, which *is* column $j$.
3. **Flat scatter.** On a flat row-major buffer (@sec-mat-a1), input cell $i \cdot n + j$ moves to output position $j \cdot m + i$; write that permutation with one loop, then slice the buffer into rows.

**Invariant.** Every input cell is written to exactly one output slot and every output slot receives exactly one input cell, so the map is a bijection between the two grids — the shape changes, the multiset of values does not.
:::

::: {#fig-mat-p2-transpose}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p,
           [["1", "2", "3"],
            ["4", "5", "6"]],
           colors={(0, 0): "green", (1, 0): "green", (0, 1): "cyan", (1, 1): "cyan",
                   (0, 2): "amber", (1, 2): "amber"},
           row_labels=["r0", "r1"], col_labels=["c0", "c1", "c2"],
           cell_w=0.95, size=11)
    V.text(ax, p, 3.1, 1.0, "\u2192", color="muted")
    V.grid(ax, p,
           [["1", "4"],
            ["2", "5"],
            ["3", "6"]],
           x=3.7,
           colors={(0, 0): "green", (0, 1): "green", (1, 0): "cyan", (1, 1): "cyan",
                   (2, 0): "amber", (2, 1): "amber"},
           cell_w=0.95, size=11)
V.show(draw)
```

The $2 \times 3$ becomes $3 \times 2$: each input column (a colour) becomes an output row. Column $\{1,4\}$ is the new top row, $\{2,5\}$ the middle, $\{3,6\}$ the bottom.

:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Nested build

::: {.form-next}
Allocate `T = [[0]*m for _ in range(n)]` and, for each input cell, write `T[j][i] = a[i][j]`. Two loops, no cleverness, works for any $m \times n$. This is the definition turned directly into code and the reference the other rungs are checked against.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("transpose", "nested")
    assert str(final) == "[[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def transpose_nested(a):
    m, n = len(a), len(a[0])
    T = [[0] * m for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(m):
        for j in range(n):
            T[j][i] = a[i][j]
    return T


assert transpose_nested([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]) == [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]
assert transpose_nested([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) == [[1, 3], [2, 4]]
assert transpose_nested([[1], [2], [3]]) == [[1, 2, 3]]
assert transpose_nested([[5]]) == [[5]]
```

##### C++

```cpp
vector<vector<int>> transposeNested(vector<vector<int>>& a) {
    int m = a.size(), n = a[0].size();
    vector<vector<int>> T(n, vector<int>(m));
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j)
            T[j][i] = a[i][j];
    return T;
}
```

:::

#### Column zip

::: {.form-next}
`zip(*a)` unpacks the rows as arguments and groups the $j$-th element of each — exactly "the $j$-th column". Wrapping each group in `list` gives the transposed rows. One line, $O(1)$ Python-level loop code, and the fastest of the three in practice because `zip` is implemented in C.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("transpose", "zip")
    assert str(final) == "[[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def transpose_zip(a):
    return [list(col) for col in zip(*a)]


assert transpose_zip([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]) == [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]
assert transpose_zip([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) == [[1, 3], [2, 4]]
assert transpose_zip([[1], [2], [3]]) == [[1, 2, 3]]
for _ in range(60):
    m, n = random.randint(1, 5), random.randint(1, 5)
    M = [[r * 10 + c for c in range(n)] for r in range(m)]
    assert transpose_zip(M) == transpose_nested(M)
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment — C++ has no zip; the column-major read is the same idea
// for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) { vector<int> row; for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) row.push_back(a[i][j]); T.push_back(row); }
```

:::

#### Flat scatter

::: {.form-next}
On a row-major flat buffer, `a[i*n + j]` moves to position `j*m + i` in the $n \times m$ output. The two-dimensional scatter form below makes that index math explicit with a single loop over input cells — the version to reach for when the matrix is stored as one array (C, CUDA, a 1-D cache trick).
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("transpose", "scatter")
    assert str(final) == "[[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def transpose_scatter(a):
    m, n = len(a), len(a[0])
    flat = [0] * (m * n)
    for i in range(m):
        for j in range(n):
            flat[j * m + i] = a[i][j]
    return [flat[k * m:(k + 1) * m] for k in range(n)]


assert transpose_scatter([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]) == [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]
assert transpose_scatter([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) == [[1, 3], [2, 4]]
assert transpose_scatter([[1], [2], [3]]) == [[1, 2, 3]]
for _ in range(60):
    m, n = random.randint(1, 5), random.randint(1, 5)
    M = [[r * 10 + c for c in range(n)] for r in range(m)]
    assert transpose_scatter(M) == transpose_nested(M) == transpose_zip(M)
```

##### C++

```cpp
vector<vector<int>> transposeScatter(vector<vector<int>>& a) {
    int m = a.size(), n = a[0].size();
    vector<int> flat(m * n);
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j)
            flat[j * m + i] = a[i][j];
    vector<vector<int>> T(n, vector<int>(m));
    for (int k = 0; k < n; ++k)
        for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i)
            T[k][i] = flat[k * m + i];
    return T;
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
All three are $\Theta(mn)$ time and must allocate the $\Theta(mn)$ output (there is no smaller answer than the transposed grid itself). **Column zip** and **flat scatter** each touch every element once; the **nested build** is the same work written out. The differences are ergonomic, not asymptotic.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- A single row becomes a single column and vice-versa: `[[1,2,3]] -> [[1],[2],[3]]`, `[[1],[2],[3]] -> [[1,2,3]]`. The output shape $n \times m$ must be derived from the input, not assumed square.
- $1 \times 1$: the transpose is itself.
- Applying the transpose twice returns the original: `transpose(transpose(a)) == a`, for any shape.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Allocating $m \times n$ instead of $n \times m$.** The output has $n$ rows of length $m$. Reusing the input shape throws on any non-square matrix.
- **Reusing one row list.** `T = [[0]*m]*n` makes all $n$ rows the *same* list; writing `T[j][i]` then corrupts other rows. Use a comprehension so each row is a fresh list.
- **`zip(*a)` on an empty matrix** yields nothing, but `zip(*[[],[]])` behaves oddly; guard a $0$-row input if your caller can pass one (the stated constraints have $m,n \ge 1$).
:::

**Variants.** Rotate Image (@sec-mat-p2-rotate) composes this transpose with a row reversal (@sec-mat-a3). [LC 566 · Reshape the Matrix](https://leetcode.com/problems/reshape-the-matrix/){difficulty="Easy"} is the flat-scatter form without the transpose: read the cells in row-major order and refill an $r \times c$ grid. In-place transpose of a square grid is the strict-upper-triangle swap of Rotate Image's second form; a rectangle needs the cycle-following transpose of exercise 13.

**Try it.** Transpose a square matrix in place by swapping $a[i][j] \leftrightarrow a[j][i]$ for $j > i$ only, and check it against `transpose_nested`.
